0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I remember the first time I heard about the invention of the iPhone, back in 2007. My friend, who followed Apple products with an almost religious zeal — there were many such people in those days — entered the room and announced “This is the convergence!” We spent the next few minutes gaping in awe at the idea that every single piece of portable consumer electronics was about to be combined into a single device. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For many, it felt like a messianic moment. The iPhone was probably the last big innovation that we Americans embraced as a whole society. Everybody had an iPhone, or wanted one. Engineers loved how the thing was engineered. Humanities PhD students showed off the latest model at parties and admired the sleek design.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">¹</span><span> Kids in working class neighborhoods were glued to their iPhones in math class. It was a supercomputer in your pocket, a voice for the voiceless, the tricorder </span><em>and </em><span>the communicator from Star Trek, all that and more.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was also big money. Years before Benedict Evans wrote “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8ab7cccd-48c5-47ae-aabc-b3daed72b86b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">The smartphone is the new sun</a><span>”, every ambitious tech entrepreneur and content creator in America was in on the game. Social media — that infinitely scrolling vertical feed — was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b5f7e619-8061-4c5b-8eac-5448aab69922?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the killer app of the smartphone</a><span>, what the spreadsheet had been for the PC or e-commerce had been for the internet. In 2012, Facebook’s monster IPO kicked off a gold rush, and everyone moved to San Francisco to strike it rich. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But you didn’t need to be a tech entrepreneur in order to get in on the action. The smartphone meant far more eyeballs glued to far more screens for far more minutes of the day, and that meant dollar signs for content creators. YouTubers, Instagram fashion influencers, and Twitter activists became whole new economic classes. Old-style content businesses like newspapers and TV networks saw their doom, but also a potential lifeline. (Eventually even econ bloggers got our piece of the pie; plenty of you signed up for this blog through a scrollable app.)</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Beautiful design coupled with brilliant engineering. Technology anyone could use. Economic opportunity for the masses </span><em>and </em><span>for the elite. A way to have your ideas and opinions heard by millions of people thousands of miles away, at any hour of any day. No wonder Steve Jobs was the last technologist that everyone agreed was an American hero. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But when I recall that fateful day in 2007, I remember not joy, but a sudden surge of foreboding. That was strange, and out of character for me. I’ve always been a technophile at heart — I grew up as a hardcore Star Trek fan, and until that moment in 2007, each new marvel — broadband, the internet, the laptop computer, etc. — had felt like it was moving us toward that bold utopian future. The iPhone felt different. Some small voice in the back of my head told me: “This is a mistake.” And though I tried to ignore that voice for many years, it remained.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What was I worried about? I think some part of me knew that someday, I would end up saying something like this:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px wonderful because it was a place you could go — a complement to real life, not a substitute. The iPhone promised to put that fantasy universe in our pockets 24/7, and we would never escape. It would be </span><em>physically </em><span>possible to turn off our phones, of course, but it wouldn’t be </span><em>socially </em><span>possible — you could always touch grass, but after everyone had an iPhone, that would be the only conduit through which you could touch another human mind.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The idea of perpetually tying every human into a global hive mind tripped alarm bells. It reminded me too much of the hive minds I had seen depicted in science fiction nightmares — the Borg from Star Trek, the Blight from </span><em>A Fire Upon the Deep</em><span>, the Human Instrumentality Project from Neon Genesis Evangelion. Humans were meant to be </span><em>individuals</em><span> — unique, independent incubators of ideas and desires, not terminals or the fingers of a world-mind. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We had spent centuries trying to escape the small, localized versions of the hive mind. The printing press, the car and the telephone had offered freedom from the crushing conformity of small-town life. When broadcast television threatened to smother us with a centrally dictated monoculture, it sparked a decades-long resistance. When the internet arrived, we spent two decades using it to revel in our individuality — we made our personal websites, started blogs, joined small online communities centered around our interests. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Sometime around 2014 or 2015 we woke up to the fact that the world of the Old Internet no longer existed. “The internet” no longer meant the Web — it meant a tiny handful of big platforms. Twitter and Reddit for screaming about politics, Facebook and Instagram for being jealous of your friends’ vacation pics. Gone were the days of painting our individuality on the canvas of the Web. The platforms were the hive minds, we were the neurons, and the smartphone was the axon that kept each of us wired tight into the collective.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“‘Social media is bad,’ he typed on social media!!” This is the perpetual and instantaneous response of many of the neurons…er, people…in my timeline. Indeed, if social media is so bad, why don’t you just put down the phone? But this idea displays a fundamental misunderstanding of the nature of network effects. Suppose I decide to get off Instagram and go play pickup basketball instead. If everyone </span><em>else </em><span>is on Instagram instead of playing pickup basketball, who am I going to play with?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is an extreme and simplified example, obviously, but the intuition here comes from real research. Bursztyn et al. (2024) </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/764eb07b-004c-4399-b582-a5a8b31da194?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">have a paper</a><span> called “When Product Markets Become Collective Traps: The Case of Social Media”. Here’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ff1b82c1-a01f-4802-b75c-e16cd1ebec53?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a quick summary</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While one would typically assume that a popular product benefits its users…Bursztyn et al. find evidence of a “product market trap:” At least among the college students in this experiment, large numbers of people are </span><strong>choosing to use social media platforms they also wish didn’t exist at all</strong><span>…[T]he authors found that [subjects] would…</span><strong>be willing to pay an average of $24 to deactivate the platform on their campus</strong><span> for four weeks. This amount rose to $43 when they also included the minority of students who weren’t TikTok users. (Results for Instagram were similar and are included in the full policy brief.) [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The students said that they only stayed on TikTok because other people were on it too, and they were afraid of missing out. FOMO is not utility; it’s a bad equilibrium. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s also an impulse to do a sort of “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8d2e7702-710c-43c5-931e-c1435efe2665?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Good Tsar, bad boyars</a><span>” maneuver, where people say “it’s not the phones, it’s social media”. But this is an argument over whether guns kill people or bullets kill people. Yes, we could access social media from laptops or other stationary devices, but we could only do so for part of the day; that would force us to develop offline interactions and relationships during the other hours, like we did back in 2007. It’s the ever-present umbilical that enables — and perhaps even mandates — the replacement of in-person interaction with an online hive mind.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">²</span><span> </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In 2007 I suppressed my deep-seated doubts about smartphone technology. I am a techno-optimist, and this was just another miraculous new tool for human empowerment. And yet the two decades since 2007 seem to have only validated my misgivings, across a number of dimensions. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since I wrote about this in 2023, the evidence has only grown stronger. Here’s an experiment by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9dc85627-2408-4d5c-8a3d-de4481c14dc3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Castelo et al. (2025)</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We used a mobile phone application to block all mobile internet access from participants' smartphones for 2 weeks and objectively track compliance. This intervention </span><strong>specifically targeted the feature that makes smartphones "smart" (mobile internet)</strong><span> while allowing participants to maintain mobile connection (through texts and calls) and </span><strong>nonmobile access to the internet</strong><span> (e.g. through desktop computers). The intervention improved mental health, subjective well-being, and objectively measured ability to sustain attention; 91% of participants improved on at least one of these outcomes. Mediation analyses suggest that these improvements can be partially explained by the intervention's impact on how people spent their time; when people did not have access to mobile internet, they </span><strong>spent more time socializing in person</strong><span>, exercising, and being in nature. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Other recent experiments have </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d42c85e9-930f-4fc2-b1b6-cfc7e035ba69?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">yielded similar results</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The likeliest explanation is that there is simply something thin and insufficient about online interaction. It’s lacking in some essential emotional nutrient that human beings evolved to harvest from the physical proximity of other human beings. Perhaps it’s something cognitive — the richness of context that tells you that no, your friend’s life isn’t perfect just because they posted a cool video of their trip to Europe, and thus you don’t need to feel constantly envious and inadequate and left-out. Or perhaps it’s something physical — the tiny touch of a high-five or a hug, the simple feeling of the proximity of other human bodies. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Whatever this emotional nutrient is, our young people are starving for it, while they binge on the cheap sugar-alcohol of emoji reactions and story views. In other parts of the world, young people are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0008a2af-7e22-49e2-a00c-c9ba8990c695?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">just starting to break free of this collective trap</a><span>, but not yet in the United States.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But making teenagers sad is one thing; putting an end to the Human Age on planet Earth is quite another.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The global fertility decline is a long-standing trend. Every country that escapes poverty, urbanizes, and teaches its people to read is going to transition from a high fertility rate (5-7 children per woman) to a much lower rate. Long before the smartphone burst on the scene, most of Europe and the richer parts of East Asia had fallen below replacement-level fertility. Everyone would crack jokes about Japan not having enough kids. </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Then the 2010s came, and then the 2020s, and suddenly it wasn’t just Japan. In fact, Japan now has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0b2c3a45-eb4e-400c-9a1e-76c9b46585d2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">one of the higher fertility rates in East Asia</a><span>, at a still-catastrophic 1.15. Thailand’s fertility has reached 0.78, South Korea’s is back up to 0.92 after record levels of economic incentives for childbearing, China’s is down to 0.90 and falling. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The rest of the world isn’t far behind. India is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/276b2bc9-3c80-4227-ae75-99dc819e88a1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">below replacement</a><span>. Latin America is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0d6138a1-01a0-4b0b-9803-e84750d687cb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">starting to look like Europe</a><span>. Mexico’s fertility is below America’s. The United States, which had long resisted the low-fertility trend among rich countries, just hit a record low of 1.57. Islam is no defense; the Middle East’s fertility is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c569c67e-1df3-4489-b12a-460dc7d49caa?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">cratering</a><span>. The only region with high birth rates now is Africa, whose fertility rate has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aac8fbe5-71bb-4379-8081-8047092c7c90?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">fallen from over 7 to under 4</a><span>, and is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e9794229-30be-4247-a0f4-80a7d26bb993?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">falling much faster than anyone expected</a><span>. The world itself </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6a30ae55-167d-4adf-98e6-3c09a6cd2537?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">may already be below replacement</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why is fertility falling everywhere across the globe, to such low levels, all at once? Whatever the cause is, it can’t be something local and parochial. It can’t be the effect of America’s Great Recession, or Confucian culture, or whatever. It has to be something that has been affecting </span><em>the entire world at the same time</em><span>, and that narrows it down to a pretty short list. Covid is a potential factor, but the acceleration came in 2017 or 2018:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure And the biggest global technological change of the 2010s was the introduction of the smartphone.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s not hard to come up with a plausible theory of why smartphones might cause people to stop having children — in fact, it’s a lot easier to explain than teen unhappiness. Childbearing requires physical contact; the kind of digital interaction provided by smartphones cannot provide that contact. So when human interaction shifts to the digital realm, whether it’s social media, dating apps, chat groups, or online pornography, </span><em>fewer children result</em><span>, simply because there are fewer chances for the type of physical interaction that creates children.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And now it’s time for data. There are no actual experiments here; no one has gone around giving out iPhones to see if the recipients end up having fewer children. But we can occasionally find differences in the speed at which smartphones arrived in various places, and we can look at how that affected fertility. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That’s what Caitlyn Myers and Ezekiel Hooper do in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f4fac39e-fbb9-4cb3-ab49-ed581b9f46d7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">their new paper</a><span> “Is the iPhone Birth Control? Causal Evidence from AT&T’s 2007–2011 Carrier Monopoly”. They write:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The U.S. general fertility rate has fallen by 22% since 2007, a sustained decline not readily explained by economic conditions, contraceptive use, housing or childcare costs, or other commonly cited factors. We assess the potential role of a different shock: the diffusion of the smartphone. The U.S. rollout of the iPhone, the first modern smartphone, provides a natural experiment: from June 2007 through February 2011, the device was sold only on AT&T, allowing us to identify its effect from variation in AT&T’s mobile broadband coverage…[A]ccess to the iPhone reduced births by 4.5–8.0% at ages 15–19 and 3.2–6.6% at ages 20–24…Overall, the diffusion of the iPhone explains 33–52% of the decline in the general fertility rate among women aged 15–44. National-survey evidence on time use and sexual behavior is consistent with the iPhone reducing in-person interactions, increasing pornography use, and reducing sexual frequency.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Myers and Hooper are not the only ones to find this result. Hudson and Boedo (2026) find that teen fertility collapsed in the U.S., England, and Wales when teens shifted from physical to online interaction:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Teen fertility collapsed globally starting around 2007. This affected countries across the income and policy spectrum. This paper argues that smartphones changed how teens spend time with each other, and that this change in turn drove the collapse in teen fertility. Once enough teens are on the phone, </span><strong>being on the phone is where the peer network is; in-person time falls sharply, and with it the unstructured contact in which most unintended teen conceptions occur</strong><span>…Within the United States, terrain ruggedness variation in broadband and 4G coverage identifies a causal effect on teen fertility, and time-use diaries show in-person socializing among teens roughly halving while digital leisure roughly tripled. A parallel design for England and Wales recovers the same acceleration and the same effect of mobile coverage on teen conceptions, ruling out country-specific contraceptive-access and welfare-reform stories. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When this result came out, a lot of people were quick to dismiss it. counterargument</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But this hand-waving dismissal makes no sense. First of all, it presumes that the </span><em>level</em><span> of fertility is irrelevant — the assumption here is that there is some completely exogenous, unexplained trend driving fertility </span><em>all the way to zero</em><span> — that whatever mysterious force made people want to go from 7 kids per family to 2 kids will inevitably make them want to proceed to 0 kids. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This requires treating the pause in fertility declines from 1940 to 2010 as a temporary aberration, and the post-2010 drop as an inevitable resumption of the pre-1940 trend. It’s basically an argument that any big drop in fertility in previous centuries should make us unsurprised at the complete cessation of all childbearing activity in the future. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That’s a stretch at best. And it totally ignores the fact that the falling fertility trend before 1940 was happening for a fundamentally different reason than the more recent trend. As </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aea7fed8-b093-4bb4-861b-8ea22e288edc?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">John Burn-Murdoch explains</a><span>, the old fertility drop was due to </span><em>parents having fewer children</em><span>, while the recent drop is due to </span><em>fewer people becoming parents at all</em><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>In previous decades, the world’s fertility rate went down because couples had fewer children. Now the main reason is that there are fewer couples</strong><span>…Had US rates of marriage and cohabitation remained constant over the past decade, the country’s total fertility rate would be </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a7fbd5b5-b5e7-42a0-b87e-db3babc69601?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">higher today</a><span> than it was 10 years ago.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A pioneering </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/42d74f48-e4db-4e35-bdc1-9ca49bb11c97?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">study</a><span> by demographer Stephen Shaw shows that in the US and most high-income countries, the number of children that mothers give birth to is stable or even rising. But the proportion of women who have any children at all has fallen steeply in the past 15 years.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On top of that, Nowrasteh and Cowen ignore the fact that Myers and Hooper don’t simply look at a changing national trend; they use </span><em>spatial</em><span> evidence, looking at the different timing of fertility declines in different places. This allows them to construct a </span><em>counterfactual</em><span>. They agree that fertility still would have fallen without the iPhone, but that it fell much </span><em>faster</em><span> because of the iPhone. Simply looking at a national trend can’t refute that sort of causal evidence.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A more sophisticated argument, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7d607dd2-50bd-4bf0-8823-c1b8baa7b0c0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">advanced by Greg Ip</a><span> and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/10025734-9495-4786-9420-06461df8f442?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">some others</a><span>, is that the Great Recession explains the timing of the fertility drop. This is the notion of an “interactive confound” — perhaps the recession hit areas with higher AT&T coverage harder than areas with less coverage. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This criticism is smarter, but also ultimately unsatisfying. Myers and Hooper try very hard to control for changing local economic conditions — unemployment, median income, poverty rates, house prices, and so on. They may not have done these controls perfectly, but to simply wave at the Great Recession as the obvious alternative explanation is to pretend that Myers and Hooper did not do those controls </span><em>at all</em><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Furthermore, this counterargument is also America-centric. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b47305bb-354a-4068-ac37-56becf6478c0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Brookes (2026)</a><span> has a paper finding a very similar effect from the introduction of fast wireless data in the Faroe Islands in 2015, long after the Great Recession had ended. Nor can the Great Recession theory explain why fertility decline didn’t slow again after the recession ended. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Finally, the dismissals of Myers and Hooper’s result ignore that they have identified and demonstrated an extremely plausible </span><em>causal mechanism</em><span> for the effect they find. 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>During [the 2010s], rates of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/648331b0-5b4f-407e-a206-19b5d19c02b1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">singledom also spiked</a><span>. In countries as varied as the United States, South Korea, Turkey, Tunisia, and Finland, young adults became less likely to have a romantic partner. And this “relationship recession” seems to have fueled the post-2010 drop in fertility. According to a 2025 study published in </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/37e02cb5-2e25-4908-b6a2-d95db05f8232?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Nature</a></em><span>, mothers in most high-income countries are having about as many children as they did decades ago. Yet fertility rates are falling nonetheless, due to a steep drop in the share of women who have any children at all.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The coupling collapse can’t be explained by a sudden expansion of women’s rights; it is happening even in deeply patriarchal societies </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f544966f-98df-418f-a37e-2cf0305fe9a2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">like Saudi Arabia</a><span>. Nor is it easily attributed to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f544966f-98df-418f-a37e-2cf0305fe9a2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">economic turmoil;</a><span> </span><strong>rates of romantic partnership have fallen in both high-growth and low-growth nations</strong><span>, advanced economies and developing ones, </span><strong>countries rattled by the 2008 crisis and those largely unharmed by it</strong><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Smartphones, on the other hand, were in the right places at the right times. [emphasis mine]</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lyman Stone, who is among the most ardent advocates of the idea that social norms determine fertility, is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4ecb8f84-bd3d-4be7-aca2-68f4752e9a6c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">ready to admit that technology can change those norms</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>[I]f we think of where digital technology, and especially smartphones, fit in the long arc of history, we see that…“this time is different,” because we are seeing a genuine honest-to-God collapse in virtually all kinds of human social life, and this collapse exists across every country and cultural group that uses digital technologies (the Amish and Haredi are mostly immune, but fertility actually is falling for Amish sects that are more technology-flexible)…To that end, we should not see digital technology as a mere “accelerator of the trend.” The new selfishness </span><em>is only a viable ideology because digital technologies made it viable</em><span>. Sitting at home wouldn’t be appealing without the digital technologies!</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If Stone’s idea of a “new selfishness” is right, it hints at something more going on than just “fewer opportunities for young people to have sex”. Among all the reasons humans bore children — labor for the farm, income support in old age, religious norms, sheer accident, and so on — one of the most powerful reasons was probably to </span><em>grow your own community. </em><span>Humans need human company, and throughout most of history, the surest way to get more company was to create it yourself. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Urbanization disrupts the need to grow your own community, by giving you a community of strangers. Fertility rates have always been much lower in cities than in the countryside, and when countries become more urbanized and wealthy, their birth rates drop. But urban friends move away, or withdraw to the suburbs to have their own kids, or outgrow the friend group. The digital companions in your smartphone screen, however — the strangers who argue with you on X, the acquaintances who post their stories on Insta, the imaginary friends of TikTok, the faux lovers of OnlyFans — never desert you. Smartphones permanently short-circuit the deep-seated human need to have your kids keep you company. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So…it’s the phones.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I suspect that a lot of people simply don’t </span><em>want</em><span> it to be the phones. We want the Spirit of 2007 back. We want technology to feel unambiguously </span><em>good</em><span> again. We want to believe in Saint Steve Jobs, the last of the American techno-heroes. We among the commentariat want to believe that the innovation that has given us our social status and our high incomes was not also something that — if its effect goes unchecked — will end the human age on planet Earth. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If the data can’t be denied, we will begin to tell ourselves that it’s actually a </span><em>good </em><span>thing. Teen pregnancy is bad, right? (Let’s ignore the fact that the research shows smartphones suppressing fertility among older cohorts.) What’s wrong with fewer humans, anyway? We could all use a little elbow room, right? And won’t AI take all the jobs anyway? </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is what humanity’s remaining young people call “cope”. The end of the Anthropocene — and that’s what it means, if fertility declines are driven by the presence of technology that never goes away — is unlikely to be easy or pretty. If AI doesn’t take all the jobs, then </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b8952817-c6bc-421c-9894-b966fd21a7c4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a shrinking humanity means a world of toil</a><span> for the young people who remain. If AI </span><em>does</em><span> take the jobs, then that toil will be averted, but humanity’s end will be correspondingly weirder. Here is what I wrote last year:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Thus, dimly and through the fog, we can begin to perceive the shape of the future that the posthuman age will take. As humanity becomes more tightly bound into a single digital collective, we find that we desire offline families less and less. As we gradually abandon reproduction, there are fewer and fewer of us, forcing us to cling even more tightly to the online collective — to spend more of our time online, to take solace in the ever-denser core of the final global village. The god-mind of that collective delivers us riches undreamt of by our ancestors, but we enjoy that bounty in solitude as we wirehead into the hive mind for a bit of company.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Go outside and look up at the night sky. The stars above you are quiet. We have received no transmissions, seen no great works of stellar engineering, met no pointy-eared friends from afar. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/49cec5b3-afa9-43f1-83d5-d1c7cf961c47?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">There seems to be a Great Filter</a><span> that has scoured the Universe of intelligent life as we know it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s possible that we have now found that filter. Perhaps it’s not nukes, or bioweapons, or self-improving AI, or the intransigence of interstellar distances. Perhaps it’s simply the fact that </span><em>biological evolution does not prepare any sentient species for technological evolution</em><span>. When innovation begins, biological beings and their societies adapt and survive for a while, but as technological change accelerates, it inevitably overwhelms hardwired biology’s speed of adaptation. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The destroyer of our species won’t necessarily come in a rain of fire, an apocalyptic plague, or an armada of drones descending on us from the sky. It may be something we excitedly pay $1000 for every three or four years. All that’s required for our species to go from the masters of the Earth to a memory in the circuits of Claude is that we decide to forsake each other’s company to stare eternally into a black mirror.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><div class="subscribe-widget is-signed-up I promise it was more fun than it sounds.</span></p></div></div><div class="footnote" data-component-name="FootnoteToDOMStatic" style="line-height: 26px;display: flex;font-size: 90%;flex-direction: row;align-items: baseline;margin-bottom: 0;border-top: none;padding-top: 0;"><span class="footnote-number" style="display: block;margin-right: 6px;min-width: 24px;">2</span><div class="footnote-content" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: block;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;min-width: 10px;"><span>In fact, I think there are some drawbacks from social media that don’t really have much to do with phones. By now, the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cc7e34a3-937f-4dfa-9262-67cd6d8fd9ab?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the corrosive effects of social media on democracy</a><span> are well-documented and pretty well-established in the data. I’ve written about them many times. But I think this problem doesn’t deserve to be included in the “phones” discourse, for two reasons. First, it seems like something that has recurred throughout human history — when a new media technology comes on the scene, the first people to adopt it tend to be extremists, attention-seekers, malignant chaos agents, and rank opportunists. This was true with the printing press, and it was true with radio. A period of conflict results, after which gatekeepers reestablish themselves. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/501c3a4d-e2dd-4077-809e-633b0602e3cb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">I expect this to happen with social media</a><span>, too; it’s just another cycle of media tech. 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;">I am not a huge fan of America’s major environmental institutions. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I believe that pollution is bad and climate change is real, and I think it’s important that policymakers take that into account. But the worldview, ideology, and priorities of the green establishment strike me as significantly askew from the imperatives of economic growth and democratic accountability. So when I saw that Rachel Carson’s 1962 book, </span><em>Silent Spring</em><span>, is now marketed on the cover as “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d3deb5fd-1b85-4131-b76f-98647d3836b1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">the classic that launched the environmental movement</a><span>,” I expected to find a book that I hated. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But as is often the case, the classics are classic for a reason. Carson’s specific arguments about the over-use of pesticides are very convincing. She has an eco-modernist streak in which she endorses the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aabbe657-eba9-4df7-8a1d-1d455885ed78?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">sterilization techniques that were successfully used to fight the New World screwworm</a><span> as an alternative to spraying. Importantly, she was just factually correct to raise the point that insects’ very rapid life cycles mean that they tend to quickly evolve resistance to insecticides. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Jerusalem in particular really got pretty Carson-pilled, seeing her as someone who built her case patiently, marshaled evidence, and won.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’m a little more cynical. Despite the book having real strengths, you can also see the fatal flaws of green ideology all the way through the text. Carson repeatedly expresses a very backward-looking romantic nostalgia. She doesn’t really distinguish between actual wilderness and just old-timey farms that she thinks are picturesque. She doesn’t seem interested in economic growth or human poverty. And Jerusalem and I agree that Carson is unduly skeptical of the normal political process and the idea of just persuading elected officials to do different stuff if you want them to weigh the balance of considerations around conservation issues differently. Modern environmentalism has instead embraced the idea that true democracy somehow involves endless </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7119d4b4-ee86-441a-888f-d21ac86bce30?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">rounds of consultation and post hoc litigation</a><span>, and while I wish you could say that’s untrue to the core text, I’m not really convinced that it is. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Has the glass been half full or half empty all along? Does the green movement need to get back to its roots or does an informed approach to environmental issues need to cut loose from those roots?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We get into all of it on this week’s episode of </span><em>The Argument</em><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Watch or listen wherever you get your podcasts.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>The transcript will be available below the paywall in this post for paying subscribers.</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ca759d36-0056-4825-8294-624643c19f6e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">WATCH THE EPISODE HERE</a></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>New episodes post every Thursday. For an ad-free version and the full transcript, subscribe at </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8a589fed-79f1-4fa0-94e8-8b58a55331f5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">TheArgumentMag.com</a><span>.</span></p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>Hi, I’m Jerusalem Demsas.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Matthew Yglesias: </strong><span>I’m Matthew Yglesias.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>Welcome to </span><em>The Argument</em><span>. This week, Matt and I read </span><em>Silent Spring</em><span>, a book that launched the modern environmental movement. And I liked it way more than I thought I was going to.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Matthew Yglesias: </strong><span>Because you hate nature?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>Yeah.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Matthew Yglesias: </strong><span>Animals? Trees?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>I absolutely hate nature. I mean, in general — as someone who’s written a lot about housing and the need to build more housing, and I care a lot about transit, I’m an urbanist — I’ve been very frustrated by a lot of parts of the modern environmental movement that have been anti-modernity, anti-science in some respects. And I was expecting a lot more of that from Rachel Carson’s book, because of the movement she spawned, but…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Matthew Yglesias: </strong><span>Well, I gotta say, I mean, you flip this book open — or, in my case, read it digitally — the very first page, though, is like, “Picture a cutesy old-time farm, and the chickens are clucking, and, like, soon it’s doom,” you know?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>Yeah, it is a little insane.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Matthew Yglesias: </strong><span>And it has this very, you know, like the industrial era of Mordor is despoiling the Shire. And I was like, “All right, this is exactly what aggravates me about these people.” And it’s in there.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But most of the book is actually pretty boring. It’s a lot of very — I don’t want to say tedious — it’s a lot of very specific information about specific instances in which insecticide was sprayed in some community, and then there were some negative consequences of spraying the insecticide. There’s a little bit of herbicide spraying, a lot of insecticide spraying, and, given its reputation, it’s just kind of narrower than I thought it was going to be.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>I mean, the book sets in, as Matt says, opens up with this sort of fable about an idyllic town, and that chapter ends — and this is also the way her famous </span><em>New Yorker</em><span> piece also starts off, which is what most people probably read. I don’t think people really read this book, because of how dense it is.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the entire book is really like a scientist’s piece-by-piece case study of what she is witnessing. And she’s a scientist, so that makes sense. But the way people talk about </span><em>Silent Spring</em><span> now — I mean, even, again, this cover, “The classic that launched the modern environmental movement” — I really expected it to be this diatribe against modernity and these really far-out-there claims, but, in reality, it just seems largely correct: a bunch of statements that follow each other that are all difficult to really grapple with.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Matthew Yglesias: </strong><span>So, I guess to pull this out: The story she tells, which, I mean, I think is historically correct, is that there was a lot of development in the chemical industry associated with the World Wars. And then, after the wars, there was a push to find civilian uses for these kinds of chemicals.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">nd one of the main things that they discovered was that certain neurotoxic agents that were related to things that were used in chemical warfare in World War I could be used in attenuated forms, or lower doses, to kill insects. Because insects are small compared to mammals. They, like, absorb material from the environment through their skin, things like that. So you can spray crops with these various different things. DDT is sort of the headline chemical, and you can kill a lot of bugs this way.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And the point of the book, I guess, is that these small doses of insecticide damage birds, mammals, and humans downstream in ways that are not being accounted for correctly by the industry, the farmers, and government officials.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>And I think the context here is just that there really wasn’t widespread awareness that there was potential damage, like side effects, of widespread DDT.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Right now I’m kind of like, I went into this book sort of like, “Well, yeah, of course, duh, there might be some knock-on effects of spraying shit into the environment.” But my awareness of that is largely downstream of work by Carson to point out that this was the case. And there was a lot of denialism, both from the chemical industry but also regulators, that there was any potential risk whatsoever to wildlife and humans, etc.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I think one thing — because we’re being pretty complimentary at this point — that I’ll point out is that the book often quickly slides between various types of harm in ways that I find very persuasive, but somewhat deceptive from a more critical point of view.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Sometimes she’s talking about, “Oh, this is hurting birds.” Sometimes she’s like, “Oh, wow, doesn’t it look ugly? Isn’t there an aesthetic loss because now the beautiful trees and the verdant grasses are gone?” And then sometimes it’s like, “Well, also maybe it causes cancer, and also maybe it doesn’t work because the insects are becoming adaptive and they’re now becoming resistant to the spraying that we’re doing.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And it’s fine to make all of these specific individual claims, but I think at its core, a lot of people are mostly concerned about the impact to human life and well-being. And most of the evidence really isn’t strongest there. The evidence is mostly really strong in the “it’s hurting the ecosystem, this could eventually have knock-on effects to hurt humans, but largely it seems like it hurts some birds.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The best evidence that it hurts humans seems to be in very specific cases where there are accidents, when workers are using the chemicals improperly, or an accident happens while they’re working.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But Carson herself dies shortly after this book is published, of breast cancer. And I think that that had a really, really big impact itself on people’s understanding of this. Obviously, it’s very difficult to link where someone got cancer from. Was it a result of the chemical environment she was in? We don’t know that’s not true. But that is something that many people do believe now, and I think that link, to “this is really hurting humans,” is both the least well-supported by the evidence, but the most persuasive element of the whole book.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Matthew Yglesias: </strong><span>Well, I mean, that’s what I wanted to say. One thing about this book is that it doesn’t have a lot of really clear policy prescriptions, and she leans at the end a lot on the argument that the spraying literally doesn’t work, that insects are developing resistance.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And so, when I was a young blogger in the mid-aughts, there was a lot of discourse that was being put forward by the Competitive Enterprise Institute and some other conservative organizations. And they wanted to make people understand that Rachel Carson and her stigmatization of DDT was responsible for the deaths of millions of people by malaria in the Third World.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So, I was familiar with that discourse at that time. And it is both true that human deaths due to malaria is, in my opinion, a much bigger problem than eggshell thinning among bald eagles, which was the signature critique of DDT, but, actually, DDT resistance among mosquitoes became a huge problem by 1970. And the main reason large-scale DDT spraying was phased out wasn’t actually to save the bald eagles. It was because it wasn’t working anymore.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And so both, I think there’s both an unfair attack on Carson that was mounted about this, but also that Carson herself is not being very clear about what she’s saying at times.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>I don’t know if that’s true. I mean, I think that there are two policy-relevant claims that she’s making: One is that there are more targeted mechanisms one could use.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">She talks over and over again about how you don’t have to do this — they were literally just spraying large-scale over towns. There’s this one anecdote that she tells, which I didn’t personally look into the veracity of — our fact-checker will let me know if it’s wrong — but where literally there are these low-flying aircraft that are just dropping all across various parts of this town without telling anyone. So people kind of freak out. They’re like, “Why are these planes really low over whatever?”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And so, that sort of thing, it’s not targeted at all. And then she points to evidence that there’s ways to target the spraying on specific crops that you’re trying to accurately — or specific weeds or herbs that you’re trying to kill, or the places where you really don’t want insects because it’s going to hurt agriculture.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The second policy-relevant claim she makes — and I find this one actually really revealing — is that you could introduce other natural elements into the ecosystem. So, for instance, bugs that would eat the insects, or moths that would eat the insects, or whatever.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I find this super interesting, because the larger claim that she has — the ecological claim she’s making — is that there’s some sort of natural equilibrium that a biosystem will eventually reach if you just “let it be the way it’s supposed to be.” I’m doing air quotes for our auditory listeners.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Matthew Yglesias: </strong><span>That’s what I mean, though. I feel like a lot of the book is this kind of motte and bailey, where — I always forget which one is the motte and which one is the bailey.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>I don’t know either.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Matthew Yglesias: </strong><span>But I think the motte is that the pesticide industry is out of control, that there are health risks associated with pesticides, and the regulators are not taking those risks seriously at all. And she absolutely convinced me of that. We need to think more clearly about what is happening and why, and for what benefit and at what cost.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But then, there’s this bailey, which is that there’s a natural balance in the ecosystem, there’s the old ways, and that these chemical disruptors are toying with it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It reminds me of the implicit politics of </span><em>Frankenstein</em><span>, right? That we’ve messed with forces that are beyond our control, and there’s going to be hell to pay for this. And notably, the cover of the book, if you hold it up — this is not a sick person; it’s a bird, right?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And a question that — you know, if I could resurrect her, or would have for you, or for anybody — is, insofar as there is a balance between producing food for the rapidly growing human population of the second half of the 20th century and birds: shouldn’t we side with the people?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>I agree that — I mean, this is again why I expected not to like this book, because I sort of assumed that it was going to come much harder on this question and be like, “Obviously I don’t care about humans as much as I care about general wildlife.” She doesn’t — I mean, just to stick to the text — she doesn’t say any of that. Social Security Trustees released their </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fffda832-ca1c-42d4-a4b6-bb3a7b97ac07?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">latest report</a><span> on the system’s finances. The numbers didn’t change much: Unless something is done, the Old Age Survivors and Disability Insurance (OASDI) program, Social Security’s official name, will be unable to pay full benefits starting in either 2032 or 2034, depending on some technical issues. That’s not far away: If the Trustees are right, the prospect of a Social Security crisis will loom over the next presidential administration.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s important to understand, however, the nature of the looming crisis. It won’t be an economic crisis. It won’t even be a serious fiscal crisis. Whatever you may have heard, Social Security isn’t in danger of going bankrupt.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What we’re facing, instead, is potential political crisis. Congress and the White House could easily take action to sustain America’s retirement system. But given the current state of our politics, there’s no guarantee that they will.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There is a widespread misunderstanding of how Social Security works. While Social Security was designed to look like a pension fund, it isn’t. A pension fund pays benefits out of a stock of assets it has accumulated over time. In contrast, Social Security operates as a government transfer program, like food stamps or Medicaid.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Now, unlike food stamps — but like the highway trust fund — Social Security is on paper supported by a dedicated tax, the payroll tax, that is assigned to that program. But I say “on paper” because from an economic point of view assigning the payroll tax to Social Security is just an accounting convention. What matters for the U.S. economy is the overall balance between government spending and government revenue, not the difference between one type of spending and one source of revenue. So there’s no inherent economic significance to the fact that by 2034 payroll tax receipts will be insufficient to cover promised benefits.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There is, however, a legislative issue. As long as the Social Security Administration can pay benefits out of payroll taxes and its cash reserve, there’s no need for Congress to vote each year to authorize benefits — they just keep going out until further notice. However, once those resources become insufficient, benefits will fall —by 17 percent according to the Trustees — unless Congress passes new legislation that “tops up” Social Security’s finances.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Yet the current administration and Republican party are such extremists that there is a real risk that Social Security will be held hostage on behalf of their goals. If this should come to pass, the hostage-takers will claim that shoring up Social Security is unaffordable. Right on cue, Mike Johnson, the Trump-sycophant Speaker of the House, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7fc1fc67-e3c9-4bed-8fb5-0ac4c13f9cbe?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">declared</a><span> on Monday that “entitlement programs” like Social Security “have to be adjusted and fixed,” and that Republicans will introduce a plan to that effect next year.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But this is a ploy, because while the cost of maintaining Social Security benefits at their promised level isn’t trivial, it is in fact affordable. According to the Trustees’ report, the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e4e475f2-4456-4449-90df-3a81a1b64a1c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">actuarial balance</a><span> of OASDI up through 2050 — the amount of additional funds it would need to keep paying full benefits for the next 25 years — is 1.06 percent of GDP. To put that number in perspective, the Trump administration proposes increasing military spending next year by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0d7deb42-fef1-47aa-a643-6adfa5272001?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">$420 billion</a><span>, equivalent to about 1.4 percent of GDP – without any discussion of whether that’s affordable</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Yet how did we get to the point where Social Security will need to be topped up? The main answer is that we have an aging population, with a growing ratio of retirees collecting benefits to workers paying into the system:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" anti-immigration policies are making this problem worse. According to the Trustees’ report, lower immigration will </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9390da23-5090-45ae-a8b7-b954d1d91d70?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">deepen</a><span> Social Security’s financial hole because many immigrants are working-age adults who will pay into the system for decades before they collect benefits. In fact, this problem may be much bigger than the report acknowledges: The report’s baseline assumption is that we’ll have net immigration of almost 1.2 million people a year, and even the pessimistic case assumes 750,000 a year. Meanwhile actual net immigration has already been cut far below that — and may now be negative.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Moreover, Social Security is being financially damaged by growing income inequality in America. Payroll taxes are levied only on wages up to $184,500, and they don’t touch capital income. With the distribution of income increasingly shifting from labor to capital, as well as becoming more unequal among wage-earners, revenue from the Social Security payroll tax has been falling as a share of national income. From 1990 to 2024, it fell from 5.02 percent of gross domestic income to 4.46 percent.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Which brings me to the question that, these days, we ask about everything: How might Social Security be affected by the advent of AI?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A short answer: If, as many of us fear, AI accelerates rising income inequality, it will further reduce the payroll tax receipts that currently pay for Social Security and further endanger its finances.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">On the other hand, if AI, as its advocates promise, leads to faster economic growth, it will increase the potential tax base that could and should be used to support Social Security and other social insurance programs. But to take advantage of that larger base, we’ll have to get serious about taxing wealth and capital income.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Is Social Security in trouble? Yes, but only because of the way its financing is currently structured — a structure that no longer works well because our society and economy have become so unequal. Moreover, Trump’s immigration policies are further endangering its already deteriorating financial condition.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So don’t believe Republicans’ gaslighting that it will be necessary to cut Social Security benefits. All that is necessary to preserve Social Security is political will to raise taxes on the wealthy and a sensible immigration policy.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">MUSICAL CODA</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Actually 67 under current law.</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/9317797c-752e-4265-b469-270b85e069e6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="margin-bottom: 0;display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/HCTunqv1Xt4" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. (Photo by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5ed2e686-a328-423a-980f-da7e37141edc?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Thing Nong Nont</a><span> via Getty Images)</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In the Los Angeles mayoral race, Nithya Raman — a left-YIMBY candidate who was in the Democratic Socialists of America but didn’t get its nomination and wasn’t supported by any of the D.S.A. members of the City Council — made it into a runoff with incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, an icon of the failed status quo in an American city that isn’t living up to its strong underlying fundamentals. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The third wheel in this race, Spencer Pratt, got a lot of attention from conservatives who don’t live in L.A. and raised some good points about problems in the city. But he fundamentally failed to even </span><em>try</em><span> to connect with actual public opinion in a place that is heavily Democratic. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Marc Novicoff (who longtime subscribers will remember from his days as Slow Boring’s very first research assistant) wrote a great piece about this </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2ca0bf24-fd33-4d9d-a125-8ef69381fc95?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">fairly depressing three-sided race</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Now that it’s down to two sides, though, there are basically two ways it could break. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One is that Bass could mobilize fear of Raman’s more out there left-wing takes to reach Pratt supporters and the kind of low-engagement part of the electorate that doesn’t vote in primaries. The other is that Raman could make good on (1) the promise of big tent YIMBYism and (2) the reality that she doesn’t actually owe anything to the institutional forces of either the status quo or the far-left and put together a unifying reform message. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I don’t know her, or the city, or the different elite actors in Southern California well enough to know exactly how she’d pull that off. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’d probably start by saying nice things about Dan Lurie in San Francisco, since he’s really the mayor who tapped into what’s good about Pratt (normie anguish about West Coast cities letting their downtowns turn into shitholes) but not into what’s bad about him (being a Republican who doesn’t actually seem like he could administer a city). </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But a really quick piece of advice I’d offer to her, or to anyone looking to moderate their image, would be to run through all their communications materials and purge mentions of “public safety” in favor of the word “crime.” </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><div purely linguistic questions tend to be a bit overrated in politics. What matters most is what elected officials do and the substantive positions that they take. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But crime really is a topic where </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ad6a055a-c1e2-4c89-b05c-f1f56139eaae?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">most jurisdictions’ outcomes are now improving</a><span> and most politicians have walked away from the substance of bad ideas. That’s all great, but it also means that it makes sense to try to talk like a normal person. All of the ideas Raman embraces under the heading of “public safety” are about crime. These are not proposals about traffic calming or coyote attacks or mudslides or </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/663de58e-85fe-4b6f-8848-9629147f7bd2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">anvils falling out of the sky in “Looney Tunes.”</a><span> If Raman wants to build a broad anti-Bass coalition, she needs to talk like a person who has some sympathy for the substance of Pratt voters’ concerns. And that means moving beyond the euphemisms coined in the progressive NGO complex.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">A euphemism that’s outlived its usefulness</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Many conservatives are excessively hung up on stuff that happened six years ago relative to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aef146fe-2fc1-4b16-b453-7ee6f0acb5e6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">egregious conduct by the current ruling coalition</a><span>. But in Democratic Party circles, nobody wants to explicitly talk about how crazy things got in 2020. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One aspect of this is that it became conventional wisdom, briefly, that anyone talking about crime as a problem was just doing racism. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This became an issue almost immediately for politicians, often themselves African-American, who represented relatively high-crime neighborhoods and whose constituents very much did worry about crime. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">As crime started rising in 2020, it was untenable to be totally indifferent to these concerns. And so “public safety” arose as a constructive intervention in the discourse. A person could talk about “public safety” to signal that they weren’t one of those bad tough-on-crime racists, but also weren’t one of those LARPing gentrifiers or out-of-touch suburbanites who had no idea what was going on.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Similarly, even when progressives stopped talking about crime, they didn’t stop supporting gun control. So they needed a way to express the idea that it’s bad when people shoot each other, and “gun violence” stepped into the fray.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size:
