circumstances of 2020, this all worked out well enough. Joe Biden and mainstream Democrats did not come out for defunding the police. Neither did the mayors of most large cities. And while the reaction to the 2020 crime jump was too slow, it wasn’t like the 1970s and 1980s when we had a generational increase in crime. Most jurisdictions pretty quickly decided to take “public safety” seriously, and in 2022 the numbers started turning around. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But even if we accept “public safety” as a useful rhetorical tool, this is like a ladder that we now need to kick away. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Raman doesn’t need to avoid cancellation from the progressive NGO borg. She needs to persuade Angelenos hungry for change that her version of a pro-housing L.A. government doesn’t mean every neighborhood will turn into Skid Row. That calls for being specific and addressing voters’ full range of concerns.</p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Lots of kinds of crime are bad </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Murder is both the worst crime and also the one that is measured most precisely, so people rightly pay a lot of attention to statistics around murder and related crimes of violence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But part of the utility of the word “crime” is that it speaks to a broader set of concerns than just violence, but also something more specific than “safety.” When I stayed in Downtown L.A. over Christmas a few years ago, I witnessed more than one person peeing on the sidewalk. This is illegal (I assume) but while I’m sure it would make some people feel unsafe, I have enough experience with urban living that I wasn’t particularly frightened by street urinators. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Nonetheless, like most people, I prefer not to walk around on streets that smell like urine. There’s a lot of cool stuff in D.T.L.A. and a lot of opportunity to convert more surface parking lots into apartment buildings and shops and make it a place with even more cool stuff. But the street urinators are bad for business over and above any objective threat to “safety.” The guys camped out in Pershing Square make the park less useful for its main purpose as a location for recreation. The guy I saw passed out in front of the Dunkin’ who was adjacent to a pool of (presumably his own) vomit wasn’t physically threatening; he was incapacitated. But those scenes are not a good advertisement for mixed-use transit-oriented developments. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">More broadly, while progressives are interested in linkages between crime and poverty, I think they mostly get the direction of causation wrong.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’m rich, so while I’m annoyed that I’ve had two e-bikes stolen in D.C., it’s not the end of the world. But property theft can be devastating if you’re poor. If your car gets stolen and you can’t get to work on time and you lose your job, that’s a disaster. If a small business needs to invest in extensive anti-theft measures, that means it’s harder for them to expand. If a neighborhood’s stores suffer from extensive shoplifting, then stores are less likely to open, so residents have fewer job opportunities. The McDonald’s by my house has removed all the chairs from its dining room because they had been so frequently occupied by vagrants and it became impossible for the restaurant to enforce the rules against loitering. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I can survive without a sit-down McDonald’s experience, but it does deprive people in the area of what’s probably the cheapest “dining out with the kids” experience. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">All the way on the other end of the spectrum, there’s a broad terrain of Rich Guy Crimes that Republicans don’t care about. But large-scale tax evasion is a serious problem. The only way to pull this off, really, is to own a business, so G.O.P. indulgence of tax cheats ultimately shifts more and more fiscal burden onto the shoulders of normal people with normal jobs. That’s bad even if it doesn’t impair “public safety.” </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We just have a lot of rules in society that make things functional — you need to pay your taxes, you can’t pee on the street — even if the individual instances are not as serious as murder. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Something we’ve seen in recent years with shoplifting is that there are tipping points: Once word got out on social media that chain store employees weren’t going to physically intervene to stop people from stealing, the formerly minor problem of small-scale retail theft became a bigger problem. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s why crime, broadly, is bad. If you don’t think something should be a crime, then that’s fine — make it legal to smoke marijuana. But if there’s a fare to ride the bus, then people who don’t pay the fare should be punished. Don’t commit crimes!</p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Who are you listening to?</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, some on the left are still loud-and-proud police de-funders or prison abolitionists. But for candidates who aren’t, and </span><em>especially</em><span> for candidates who hopped on the anti-enforcement bandwagon but want to convince voters that they’ve seen the error of their ways, I think the very utility of the “public safety” euphemism is why it’s now obsolete. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What we’re talking about, essentially, is a verbal formula designed to ward off criticism from progressive groups and nonprofits. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But what someone in Raman’s position wants to do is ward off concerns that she’ll be excessively responsive to those groups. When Zohran Mamdani said he no longer believed the things he’d said about crime and policing in 2020, enough people believed him to win an election in New York City, but lots of people didn’t believe him. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Then he retained the former administration’s police commissioner, crime continued to fall in his first months in office, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2a1ab636-3969-4f5b-913b-5ff5b5c329b7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">and the N.Y.P.D. grew in size</a><span>. This has now become a topic that is beyond the level of speculating about what he “really” believes and whether he’s “really” changed his mind — a politician is what he does, and what Mamdani is doing is acting like a person who cares more about reducing crime than he does about avoiding criticism from anti-enforcement leftists. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There was a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e80a8373-5c47-4412-b8b4-d76beb72fc16?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">bizarre piece in Gothamist recently</a><span> about extra officers getting deployed to high-crime neighborhoods in the Bronx that takes until the 29th paragraph — after many quotations of left-wing professors and activists — to share the perspective of a guy who lives in the area and is excited about the idea of more cops on the beat. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The key thing is that Mamdani clearly does not care at this point if a reasonable tactical decision draws unreasonable criticism from unreasonable people. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And politicians need to use rhetoric that conveys their lack of interest in these unreasonable people. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Back in the summer of 2020, when I was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1e6d5491-b9c3-4ad3-bdc0-d1f36fcc8032?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">saying that policing reduces crime</a><span> at a time when that was an unfashionable take, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/551fa7f0-6239-495f-9ac2-1300d4e7bf0a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Alec Karakatsanis rebutted me with an article</a><span> arguing that the whole idea of “crime” is a mistaken framing. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s a certain intellectual consistency to that. The abolitionists sincerely reject the whole ordinary language construct of “crime.” Most people, though, do think it’s a real thing and want politicians to talk about it plainly, which is a reason that saying that police reduce crime by arresting criminals and deterring others from committing crimes is a powerful formula.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Of course, there are other things besides punishment and deterrence that you can and should do to help people in troubled situations. But we in fact know that people from all walks of life commit crimes for financial gain when they think they can get away with it, and purely focusing on social service delivery will no more stop shoplifting rings or drug crews than it will stop tax evasion or Medicare fraud. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Fight crime!
